blocks.text: 验证闭环是让你能把更多工作交给 Claude 的基础。没有它，你基本上只能同时跑一两个 Claude，因为所有东西都得自己检查。有了它，你可以并行跑几十甚至上百个。

blocks.text: 这是因为给智能体一个验证其输出的途径，是提升质量的有效方法。在围绕结构化文件生成的内部测试中，让一个独立的评分器按评分标准检查 Claude 的工作，相比标准的提示词循环，任务成功率最多提升了 10 个百分点，而且在最难的问题上收益最大。

blocks.text: 无论选择哪种测试类型，都有几种失败模式要避免。

blocks.text: 如果测试不稳定，你就会把智能体训练成重跑测试，而不是去修出错的代码。如果测试很慢，智能体在批次之间做的测试就会更少，这会让你难以定位问题。较重的测试最好在提交改动之前运行。

blocks.text: 端到端测试

inlines.text: 端到端测试

blocks.text: 如果只能专注一类测试，那就选端到端。这类测试描述真实的用户流程，比如把商品加入购物车、结账、跳转到确认页。

inlines.text: 如果只能专注一类测试，那就选端到端。这类测试描述真实的用户流程，比如把商品加入购物车、结账、跳转到确认页。

blocks.text: 端到端测试之所以有效，是因为它很难被糊弄——要么整个功能能用，要么不能用。它还有明确的完成标准，能具体告诉你哪里坏了。

blocks.text: 很多测试都是基于你预想中可能出问题的地方来设计的。而属性测试关注的是人们容易忽略的边界情况，智能体往往正是在这些地方出错。

blocks.text: 几乎每个软件项目里都有大量属性，比如：

inlines.text: 几乎每个软件项目里都有大量属性，比如：
往返编码
：“把 X 编码后再解码，得到的还是 X。”解析和序列化同样适用。
不变量
：必须始终成立的东西，比如“账户余额永远不会变成负数”。
幂等性
：同一个操作（迁移、归一化、重试）执行两次和执行一次效果相同。
等价性
：优化后的代码与朴素但正确的代码产生相同结果。

blocks.text: 属性测试库用边界情况来检验智能体是否诚实可靠，而这些边界情况不会带着与生成原始代码的智能体相同的偏见。在重写场景中，它们尤其有用——此时规格说明已经偏离生产环境的行为，不再是可靠的验证依据。

blocks.text: 差分测试：以旧系统为准绳

inlines.text: 差分测试：以旧系统为准绳

blocks.text: 差分测试在功能预期保持不变的大规模迁移场景中尤其有效。做法是用相同的输入分别运行旧系统和新系统，看结果是否不同。如果不同，就说明存在需要修复的 bug 或破坏性变更。

blocks.text: 差分测试的关键在于使用随机生成的输入或生产流量样本。你还需要归一化空白字符等无关因素，并维护一份已批准的变更清单，用于新环境本就应当与旧环境不同的情况。

blocks.text: 在 Claude Code 仓库中，我们有两种把漏报案例转化为规则的方法。第一种是从人工代码审查评论和 PR 回滚中提取模式，找出常见问题。这些问题必须至少出现在两个 PR 中，并且能从 diff 中识别出来，才能被视为潜在规则。会有三个智能体尝试证伪它们，然后由人工在 PR 中审查并批准。

blocks.text: Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.

blocks.text: That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.

blocks.text: What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.

blocks.text: You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.

blocks.text: No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.

inlines.text: No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.

blocks.text: If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes.

blocks.text: E2E tests

inlines.text: E2E tests

blocks.text: If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.

inlines.text: If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.

blocks.text: The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you what’s broken.

inlines.text: The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you what’s broken.

blocks.text: Property tests: constraints that can’t break

inlines.text: Property tests: constraints that can’t break

blocks.text: A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.

blocks.text: You start by writing a statement you think can’t fail and then use a test library (fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise.

blocks.text: There are many properties in virtually every software project like:

inlines.text: There are many properties in virtually every software project like:
Round-trip encoding
: “if you encode X then decode it back, you get X.” This works for parsing and serialization as well.
Invariants
: Things that must always be true, like “account balance can never become negative.”
Idempotency
: Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once.
Equivalence
: Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code.

blocks.text: Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that aren’t created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification.

blocks.text: Differential tests: the old system is the oracle

inlines.text: Differential tests: the old system is the oracle

blocks.text: Differential tests are particularly effective for large-scale migration use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.

large-scale migration

use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed.

blocks.text: The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. You’ll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old.

blocks.text: We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work.

blocks.text: Verification means running the change

inlines.text: Verification means running the change

blocks.text: Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.

inlines.text: Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude.

blocks.text: Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.

inlines.text: Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work.

blocks.text: To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes.

blocks.text: Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid.

blocks.text: When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic.

blocks.text: Reliability checks trigger on the diff

inlines.text: Reliability checks trigger on the diff

blocks.text: We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is “--resume loads old transcripts.” When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won’t have it.

One is “--resume loads old transcripts.” When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts won’t have it.

blocks.text: Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches–usually 3 to 10–so nobody has to memorize past outages.

blocks.text: We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code.

blocks.text: We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It’s cheaper and finds more.

blocks.text: Changes can't modify their own checks

inlines.text: Changes can't modify their own checks

blocks.text: If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes. The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify.

never from the pull request's changes

blocks.text: The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.

blocks.text: The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite.

blocks.text: We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes.

blocks.text: Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck – Claude Code isn't perfect.

blocks.text: Test your checks on what actually matters

inlines.text: Test your checks on what actually matters

blocks.text: The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

inlines.text: The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean.

blocks.text: This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post, we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system.

blocks.text: They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance.

blocks.text: In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit.

blocks.text: Turn misses into rules

inlines.text: Turn misses into rules

blocks.text: In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR.

blocks.text: The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md.

blocks.text: Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why.

inlines.text: GOOD TESTS, GOOD RESULTS

blocks.text: We’ve found that giving your agent a way to verify its work with a strong feedback loop makes all the difference. Treat your verification layer like you would any other system. Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesn’t happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running.

Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesn’t happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running.

blocks.text: Do that and your job shifts from reading every diff to defining what “done” looks like and reviewing the evidence, which is what lets you run many Claudes at once.
